claims.text: A Ti–Ni-primary high-entropy alloy can be formulated with approximately 35 at% Ti, 35 at% Ni, and Cr, Mo, and Fe as the other three constituents.
Solutionizing at 1200°C for 1 hour followed by quenching and aging at 750°C for 10 hours will induce Ti–Ni intermetallic precipitation.
Solutionizing at 1200°C ensures a homogenized solid solution in the proposed alloy.
The specified aging treatment produces uniformly distributed nanoscale Ti–Ni intermetallic precipitates.
The Ti–Ni intermetallic precipitates produced by aging are coherent with the alloy matrix.
Finely dispersed coherent Ti–Ni precipitates impede dislocation motion at elevated temperatures.
Impeded dislocation motion increases elevated-temperature yield strength.
The precipitates slow elevated-temperature creep deformation.
The aged alloy will have significantly higher elevated-temperature yield strength than an as-cast or solely solution-treated baseline.
The aged alloy will have a lower elevated-temperature creep strain rate than an as-cast or solely solution-treated baseline.
Departures from the prescribed aging schedule may cause excessive precipitate coarsening or dissolution.
Exposure to sufficiently high service temperatures may cause rapid coarsening or dissolution of the precipitates.
Long-term coarsening or dissolution of the precipitates would undermine their strengthening effect.
Yield strength, creep strain rate at 750°C, and precipitate morphology and coherency can be compared between aged and solution-treated samples.

contradictions.description: The comparator is not defined consistently: it is variously called untreated, as-cast, solely solution-treated, or only solution-treated. These states can have different microstructures and properties, so they are not interchangeable controls.
